cards.definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to a known target using labeled examples.
cards.useCase: Needs a label on every training row, so data with no target column cannot be used.
cards.example: Emails labeled spam or not spam

cards.definition: The column holding the known answer that the model learns to predict.
cards.useCase: Everything else in the table is a candidate feature.

cards.definition: Supervised learning where the target is a category.
cards.useCase: Scored with accuracy, precision, recall and F1.

cards.definition: Supervised learning where the target is a number on a continuous scale.
cards.useCase: Scored with MSE and R-squared.

cards.definition: The labeled rows (about 70-80%) the model learns from.
cards.useCase: Fit the model on these rows only.

cards.definition: Labeled rows (about 20-30%) held back to judge the model on unseen data.
cards.useCase: Never learn from them, or the score is not fair.

cards.definition: A count of predictions by actual and predicted class: TP, FP, FN, TN.
cards.useCase: Every classification metric is computed from these four numbers.

cards.definition: A negative row that the model wrongly calls positive: a false alarm.
cards.useCase: Precision drops as false positives rise.
cards.example: A genuine purchase blocked as fraud

cards.definition: A positive row that the model wrongly calls negative: a miss.
cards.useCase: Recall drops as false negatives rise.
cards.example: A sick patient cleared as healthy

cards.definition: (TP + TN) / all rows: the share of predictions that were right.
cards.useCase: Misleading when one class is rare.

cards.definition: TP / (TP + FP): of the rows flagged positive, the share that really were.
cards.useCase: Prioritize it when a false alarm is costly.

cards.definition: TP / (TP + FN): of the truly positive rows, the share that were found.
cards.useCase: Prioritize it when a miss is costly.

cards.definition: 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall), the harmonic mean of the two.
cards.useCase: One number when both kinds of error matter; low if either is low.

cards.definition: A dataset where one class is far rarer than the other.
cards.useCase: Accuracy can look high while the rare class is never found; check recall and F1.

cards.definition: The average of the squared gaps between actual and predicted values.
cards.useCase: Lower is better; large misses count heavily. RMSE is its square root.

cards.definition: The share of the target's variance a model explains: 1 is perfect, 0 equals predicting the mean.
cards.useCase: Can be negative on test data for a model worse than the mean.

cards.definition: How well a model performs on new data it has not seen.
cards.useCase: The aim of every evaluation step.
cards.example: Test score close to training score

cards.definition: High training score but much lower test score: noise has been memorized.
cards.useCase: Fix with a simpler model, more data, pruning or regularization.

cards.definition: Low scores on both training and test data: the model is too simple.
cards.useCase: Fix with a more flexible model or better features.

cards.definition: Bias: error from over-simple assumptions. Variance: sensitivity to the particular training sample.
cards.useCase: Underfitting is high bias; overfitting is high variance.
cards.example: A straight line on a curve: high bias

cards.definition: Split into k folds and train k models, each validating on a different fold; average the scores.
cards.useCase: A steadier estimate than one split, and every row is validated once.

cards.definition: k-fold where every fold keeps the class proportions of the full data.
cards.useCase: Use when classes are imbalanced.

cards.definition: k-fold with k equal to the number of rows: one row validates, the rest train.
cards.useCase: Only for very small datasets; one model per row.

cards.definition: Validation that always trains on the past and tests on the future, without shuffling.
cards.useCase: For data ordered in time, so the model never learns from the future.

cards.definition: Predicts from the k closest training points: a majority vote for classes, an average for numbers.
cards.useCase: Simple, no training step; needs scaled features.
cards.example: k = 5: three neighbors are class A, so A

cards.definition: An algorithm that builds no model in training and defers the work to prediction.
cards.useCase: That makes prediction slow on large datasets.
cards.example: KNN stores the rows and measures distances later

cards.definition: Straight-line distance: the square root of the sum of squared gaps.
cards.useCase: The usual default distance.

cards.definition: The sum of the absolute gaps along each axis, like street-grid blocks.
cards.useCase: Cheaper to compute: no squares or square root.

cards.definition: Small k follows noise (overfit); large k blurs groups toward the majority class (underfit).
cards.useCase: Pick k by cross-validation; use an odd k for two classes.
cards.example: Try 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and keep the best CV score

cards.definition: Rescaling features so that none dominates the distance.
cards.useCase: Do it before KNN, K-Means and other distance-based methods.

cards.definition: A model that asks a chain of feature tests and ends in a prediction at a leaf.
cards.useCase: Readable as rules; needs no scaling.
cards.example: If income > 50k and age < 30, then class A

cards.definition: Root: the first test. Internal node: a test on one feature. Leaf: the final prediction.
cards.useCase: Rows are routed down branches until they reach a leaf.

cards.definition: 1 minus the sum of squared class shares: 0 for a pure node, 0.5 for an even two-class mix.
cards.useCase: The tree picks the split with the lowest weighted Gini.

cards.definition: A measure of mixing: minus the sum of p x log2(p). 0 for a pure node, 1 bit for an even two-class mix.
cards.useCase: An alternative to Gini for choosing splits.

cards.definition: The drop in entropy from a parent node to its weighted children.
cards.useCase: The split with the largest gain wins.

cards.definition: Cutting branches or capping depth so a tree cannot memorize the training rows.
cards.useCase: The main defense against decision-tree overfitting.

cards.definition: Combining many models so that the joint prediction beats any single one.
cards.useCase: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees.

cards.definition: Many decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets, combined by vote or average.
cards.useCase: More accurate and stable than one tree, but harder to read.

cards.definition: Rows drawn at random with replacement to train one tree.
cards.useCase: Makes each tree see a different version of the data.
cards.example: Row 7 appears twice, row 9 not at all

cards.definition: At each split a tree may consider only some of the features.
cards.useCase: Keeps the trees different so their errors cancel.

cards.definition: Rows left out of a tree's bootstrap sample (about one third).
cards.useCase: Provide a free validation estimate for that tree.
cards.example: Score each tree on its unseen rows

cards.definition: Predicts a number as an intercept plus a weighted sum of several features.
cards.useCase: Assumes a straight-line relationship, independent errors with constant spread, and little multicollinearity.

cards.definition: The change in the prediction for a one-unit rise in one feature, holding the others constant.
cards.useCase: An association within the model, not proof of cause.
cards.example: -35 per km from the center: rent falls by 35

cards.definition: The predicted value when every feature is 0.
cards.useCase: The starting point of the equation.

cards.definition: The actual value minus the predicted value.
cards.useCase: Residuals should be centered on zero with no pattern and constant spread.

cards.definition: Two or more features strongly correlated with each other.
cards.useCase: Makes coefficients unstable, with sizes swinging and signs flipping; drop or combine features.

cards.definition: A score showing how well a feature is predicted by the other features.
cards.useCase: Values above roughly 5-10 signal multicollinearity.

cards.definition: R-squared that is penalized for each extra feature.
cards.useCase: Plain R2 never falls on the training data when a feature is added.
cards.example: Adding a random column lowers it

cards.definition: A classifier that outputs a probability from 0 to 1, then applies a threshold.
cards.useCase: Despite the name, it predicts categories, not numbers.

cards.definition: Learning from data with no target labels, looking for structure in the features.
cards.useCase: Cannot be checked against an answer key.

cards.definition: Grouping rows so that members resemble each other more than members of other groups.
cards.useCase: The most common unsupervised task.

cards.definition: Describing the data with fewer features while keeping as much information as possible.
cards.useCase: Unsupervised, along with clustering. PCA is the standard example.

cards.definition: Hard: each point in exactly one cluster. Soft (fuzzy): a degree of membership in several.
cards.useCase: Soft clustering suits points that sit between groups.

cards.definition: Centroid-based (K-Means), connectivity-based (hierarchical), density-based (DBSCAN).
cards.useCase: Choose by cluster shape and by whether you know k.

cards.definition: Forms k clusters by assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to their means until stable.
cards.useCase: You choose k first; it assumes round, similar-sized clusters.

cards.definition: The mean position of the points in a cluster.
cards.useCase: Moves each iteration until assignments stop changing.

cards.definition: The sum of squared distances from each point to its own centroid.
cards.useCase: Lower means tighter clusters, but it always falls as k grows.

cards.definition: A plot of inertia against k; the best k sits at the bend where the drop levels off.
cards.useCase: A visual way to choose k.
cards.example: Sharp drop to k = 4, then flat: choose 4

cards.definition: A smarter start for the centroids, and reruns from different starts keeping the lowest inertia.
cards.useCase: K-Means can settle in a poor local optimum depending on its start.

cards.definition: A centroid is a mean, so an extreme point drags it off the cluster's center.
cards.useCase: Remove outliers or use a method such as DBSCAN; also scale features first.
cards.example: One huge value skews a cluster

cards.definition: Bottom-up: every point starts as a cluster and the two closest are merged, repeatedly.
cards.useCase: No need to choose k in advance.
cards.example: Merge 1 and 2 first, then the next closest

cards.definition: Top-down: start with one cluster and split it repeatedly.
cards.useCase: The reverse of agglomerative.
cards.example: One cluster splits into two, then four

cards.definition: A tree of merges; the height of each join is the distance at which the merge happened.
cards.useCase: Cut it with a horizontal line: the lines crossed are the clusters.
cards.example: A cut across 4 lines gives 4 clusters

cards.definition: Single: distance between the closest pair of points. Complete: between the farthest pair.
cards.useCase: Single tends to chain; complete gives compact clusters.

cards.definition: Average: mean distance over all pairs. Ward: merge the pair that raises within-cluster variance least.
cards.useCase: Ward gives compact, K-Means-like clusters.

cards.definition: Density-based clustering: clusters are dense regions separated by sparse ones; sparse points are noise.
cards.useCase: No k needed; finds any shape and flags outliers.

cards.definition: The radius of the neighborhood around a point.
cards.useCase: Too small leaves much noise; too large merges clusters.

cards.definition: How many points must lie within eps for a point to count as a core point.
cards.useCase: A higher value is stricter and creates more noise.

cards.definition: Core: dense. Border: within eps of a core but not dense. Noise: reachable from no core.
cards.useCase: Noise is labeled -1 and left unassigned.
cards.example: A lone point far from everything

cards.definition: Struggles when clusters differ greatly in density, and is sensitive to eps.
cards.useCase: Use a k-distance plot to choose eps, and scale the features.
cards.example: A tight cluster beside a loose one

cards.definition: Builds fewer new, uncorrelated features (components) that keep as much variance as possible.
cards.useCase: Unsupervised dimensionality reduction; it ignores the target.

cards.definition: A weighted blend of all the original features. The first points along the greatest variance.
cards.useCase: Components are perpendicular and ordered by variance.

cards.definition: The share of the total variance that each component holds.
cards.useCase: Add them up until you reach a goal such as 90-95% to choose how many to keep.

cards.definition: A plot of the explained variance of each component in order.
cards.useCase: Stop where the curve flattens.

cards.definition: PCA chases variance, so features in large units would dominate unless scaled.
cards.useCase: Standardize first, then fit PCA.

cards.definition: PCA is unsupervised and maximizes variance. LDA uses the labels to maximize class separation.
cards.useCase: Both reduce dimensions; only LDA needs the target.
cards.example: PCA to compress, LDA to separate known classes

cards.definition: A neuron that computes an activation of the weighted sum of inputs plus a bias.
cards.useCase: One perceptron can only draw a straight-line boundary, so it cannot learn XOR.

cards.definition: A learned number that scales how strongly one input influences a neuron.
cards.useCase: A weight near 0 means that input has almost no influence.

cards.definition: A learned constant added to the weighted sum that shifts where a neuron activates.
cards.useCase: Weights and biases are the parameters that training changes.

cards.definition: A non-linear function applied to a neuron's sum so the network can learn curves.
cards.useCase: Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear transformation.

cards.definition: ReLU: max(0, x). Sigmoid: 0 to 1. Tanh: -1 to 1. Softmax: probabilities summing to 1.
cards.useCase: ReLU for hidden layers; sigmoid for two classes; softmax for many classes.

cards.definition: Data enters the input layer, passes through hidden layers, and the prediction leaves the output layer.
cards.useCase: Input neurons = number of features. Deep learning means two or more hidden layers.

cards.definition: Parameters (weights, biases) are learned. Layers, neurons and learning rate are set beforehand.
cards.useCase: Count a dense layer's parameters as inputs x neurons + neurons.

cards.definition: A score of how far the predictions are from the true targets.
cards.useCase: Training tries to make it small. MSE for regression, cross-entropy for classification.

cards.definition: Pushing inputs through the layers to get a prediction.
cards.useCase: The first step of each training iteration.

cards.definition: Finds the gradient of the loss for every weight and bias by working backward with the chain rule.
cards.useCase: It supplies the gradients; gradient descent uses them.
cards.example: Output error flows back to earlier layers

cards.definition: Repeatedly nudges each weight against its gradient to reduce the loss.
cards.useCase: w_new = w_old - learning rate x gradient.

cards.definition: The step size that scales each gradient descent update.
cards.useCase: Too large overshoots and the loss bounces; too small is very slow.

cards.definition: Epoch: one pass over all training data. Batch: all rows per update. Mini-batch: a small group per update.
cards.useCase: Mini-batch is the usual compromise between one row and all rows.
